extracted.intended_audience: cognitive neuroscientists, psychologists, and researchers studying humor, creativity, and fMRI methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, running, and interpreting an fMRI experiment that contrasts real-time humorous caption generation with mundane caption generation to identify neural correlates of humor creativity and expertise effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stimulus selection: non-humorous prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Select drawings that were not funny by themselves; remove original captions and any inherently funny elements (some drawings processed with Photoshop) so the prompt does not confound generation with passive appreciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To isolate active humor generation from passive humor appreciation, use stimuli that are humor-free; this avoids confounding neural correlates of creating humor with those of appreciating funny stimuli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental conditions: HUM, MUN, NOTH
rubrics_metrics.description: Use three trial types: (1) 'Humorous' (HUM) — generate a funny caption; (2) 'Expected'/'Mundane' (MUN) — generate a mundane caption appropriate for the drawing; (3) 'Nothing' (NOTH) — view the drawing without thinking of a caption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasting HUM vs. MUN allows separation of creative/humorous processes from standard problem solving; including NOTH helps identify general visual/semantic activations via conjunction contrasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial timing and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Each trial lasts 17 s: first 2 s present a cue word indicating condition, then 15 s for the drawing presentation and caption generation; participants immediately rate their caption using a keyboard on a 4-point scale once they think of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixed timing (2 s cue + 15 s generation) permits separation of early vs. late processes; instruct participants to press/rate immediately when they have a caption to capture timing of generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant grouping and expertise coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Recruit and classify participants into Professionals (improv and stand-up), Amateurs (promising comedians), and Controls; define 'expertise' numerically as Controls = 0, Amateurs = 1, Professionals = 2 (and optionally subdivide Professionals further, e.g., Controls=0; Amateurs=1; Stand-Ups=2; Improv=3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treating the ordinal expertise scale as interval is acceptable for regression to capture linear trends, but validate with t-tests between groups; control for demographic covariates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-ratings and independent ratings of funniness
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants rate their own captions on a 4-point scale (1–4). Independent raters later judge recalled captions on a 7-point scale for funniness, cleverness, and offensiveness; ratings are normalized per rater before averaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both self and independent ratings to evaluate caption quality; normalization per rater controls for different usage of the scale and improves comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-scan recall and rater assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: After scanning, present participants with drawings from recent runs and have them recall and write down generated captions. Recruit a pool of independent raters, each rates a subset of captions (e.g., a quarter), and normalization is applied within-rater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collecting recalled captions enables independent evaluation of generated material; distribute caption rating workload across many raters to obtain robust funniness measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of early TRs to index generation vs evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Target early timepoints (e.g., TRs 4–6) to capture the process of generating a humorous caption rather than later evaluation of the fully formed caption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because generation processes occur earlier than evaluation, correlating early activation with later-rated funniness supports an interpretation that the region contributes to creation rather than post-hoc evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funniness-magnitude effect definition
rubrics_metrics.description: An ROI is considered to display a 'funniness magnitude' effect if it is localized with the HUM minus MUN contrast (i.e., humor selective) and greater activation in that ROI early in the trial predicts generation of funnier captions (by self and/or independent ratings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrating a dose-response relationship between early activation magnitude and later funniness supports a role for the region in producing higher-quality (funnier) creative outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprocessing pipeline requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform 3D motion correction (trilinear interpolation), 3D spatial smoothing using a 4-mm full-width at half-max Gaussian filter, and linear trend removal using a high-pass filter set to three cycles over the run's length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard and explicit preprocessing choices reduce noise and motion artifacts; report software used (e.g., Brain Voyager) and parameters to facilitate replication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical model specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a general linear model with a separate regressor for 12 TRs from the beginning of each trial type (so TR #1 includes the 2 s cue interval). Include the six motion correction parameters (3 translations, 3 rotations) as regressors of no interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeling the full trial time course and including motion parameters helps isolate cognitive effects and reduce confounds from subject motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: ROI localization contrasts and TR-interval analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Define ROIs using contrasts such as HUM minus MUN and HUM+MUN - 2×NOTH, and across TR-intervals (e.g., 3–6 early, 7–10 late) to capture time-dependent activations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using multiple contrasts and temporal windows permits localization of regions involved at different stages (generation vs later construction/evaluation) of humor creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: ROI statistical thresholds and correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use conservative thresholds for ROI localization: never use uncorrected p-values higher than p = 0.001 for initial exploration; for the main HUM−MUN contrast use p < 0.01 Bonferroni corrected; adjust p-values to obtain well-defined, smaller ROIs as necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying stringent corrections (e.g., Bonferroni) when defining ROIs reduces false positives and supports reliable inferences about localized activations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance and testing for double-dipping (non-independence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Localize ROIs using data from all participants with conservative thresholds and then verify results by localizing the same regions independently within each group and/or by using ROIs from an independent previous study; explicitly discuss potential non-independence biases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize how group composition (e.g., largest group shifting ROI boundaries) could bias within-ROI analyses; re-run analyses with independently localized ROIs to ensure effects are not artifacts of non-independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data acquisition reporting and matching to prior work
rubrics_metrics.description: Report scanner and sequence details (e.g., Siemens Trio 3T; structural MPRAGE TR=1100 ms, 1 mm isotropic voxels; functional EPI TR=2000 ms, TE=30 ms, flip angle=62°, in-plane resolution 3×3 mm, 3 mm slices, 32 axial slices including Temporal Poles). Match acquisition parameters to previous related studies to facilitate comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed scanner parameters help reproducibility and allow direct comparisons with prior studies examining passive humor appreciation or other creativity tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for demographic and confounding variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Include age and sex as regressors of no interest in group-level analyses; examine whether demographic variables correlate with ROI activations (e.g., maleness correlated with rTOJ activity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controlling for demographics mitigates confounds due to unequal group composition (e.g., fewer females in comedians) and clarifies whether observed effects are due to expertise or other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing group/expertise effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute regression analyses of HUM−MUN average activation across the full trial and at peak (TRs 5–7) with expertise as a predictor (report β, p-value, and Cohen's d); validate with t-tests comparing Professionals vs Controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining regression (to detect linear trends across expertise) and pairwise t-tests (to validate group differences) gives a robust assessment of expertise-related effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation criteria for brain-region functional roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Use convergence of evidence—time course, funniness-magnitude effect, expertise gradients, and prior literature—to infer roles: temporal association regions (TOJ/TP) as sites where remote associations converge (source of humorous ideas); mPFC as directing deliberate/top-down search (control); striatum as reward/expectation signal that may precede or facilitate retrieval of humorous associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret neural activations in light of timing (early vs late), correlations with outcome quality, and how effects vary with expertise rather than relying on single contrasts alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjunction contrasts to identify shared activations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use conjunctions (e.g., MUN and HUM contrasted with NOTH) to reveal additional activations common to both caption-generation tasks, such as temporal regions involved in semantic processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conjunctions help distinguish processes common to both creative and mundane caption generation (e.g., language/theory-of-mind engagement) from those specific to humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterbalancing and trial sequencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterbalance drawings across the three conditions between participants (approximate balancing if group sizes preclude perfect balance). Sequence runs with jittered trials so that each sequence of two conditions appears the same number of times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counterbalancing controls for stimulus-specific effects; jittering and balanced sequencing reduce temporal confounds in event-related designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reaction-time analysis and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure reaction times for rating captions; HUM trials show longer RTs than MUN, and professionals may have longer RTs than amateurs. Consider whether longer RTs indicate task difficulty rather than creativity and address this by focusing on early activation and funniness-magnitude correlations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer RTs alone do not establish that activation differences are due to difficulty; complement RT analysis with early-TR correlations to support generation-specific interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalization and reliability of rating scales
rubrics_metrics.description: Normalize independent raters' scores within each rater before averaging; check covariance between self-ratings and independent ratings to assess reliability and agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normalization mitigates inter-rater scale differences; reporting agreement statistics (e.g., covariance) reassures that funniness judgments are consistent across raters.
